Chapter 8: Negotiation Jujitsu — Redirecting Attacks and Breaking Deadlocks
Ever been in a negotiation where the other person digs in their heels, or comes at you with a direct attack? It’s easy to feel boxed in—or to want to push back just as hard. But here’s the thing: when you meet force with force, you almost never get a win-win.
That’s where negotiation jujitsu comes in. Think of it like the martial art—jujitsu—where instead of fighting your opponent’s energy, you use it to your advantage. In negotiation, this means you don’t go head-to-head. Instead, you invite the other person to join you in solving the problem together.
So, what are the key moves in negotiation jujitsu?
First, don’t attack their position—look behind it. Instead of pushing back, ask questions. Try to uncover what’s really driving their demands. Maybe there’s something important underneath that you both can work with.
Next, don’t defend your ideas—invite criticism and advice. If you encourage the other side to poke holes in your proposal, you’re actually getting them involved in shaping it. Suddenly, you’re not adversaries—you’re collaborators.
And here’s another: don’t reject—reframe. So, if they say, “That’s impossible,” you might ask, “What would make it possible?” It turns a dead end into a starting point for new ideas.
Sometimes, the best response is simply... silence. When someone tries to provoke you, not reacting right away can take the wind out of their sails—and give them a moment to rethink.
Let’s make this real. Imagine someone tells you, “This is our final offer.” Instead of locking horns, you could say, “Help me understand how you arrived at that figure,” or, “What would you do if you were in my shoes?” These kinds of questions invite a real conversation, not a standoff.
Negotiation jujitsu is really about keeping your cool and steering things back toward problem-solving—even when the other person is trying to pull you into an argument or a power struggle.
Now, if you’ve tried all these moves and the other side just won’t budge, it might be time to bring in a neutral third party—maybe a mediator or a facilitator. Someone who can help both sides stay focused on what really matters.
In the end, negotiation jujitsu protects you from getting drawn into fights or manipulated, while still moving toward a fair deal. It’s about turning tough moments into opportunities for real progress.
